opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think tool access is one of the core ingredients, but it's maybe not the one people expect. When folks talk about agents, they tend to focus on the model: is it smart enough, can it reason well enough? And that matters. But the way I think about it, a useful agent is roughly the product of three things: a capable model, the right context, and the right tools. If any one of those is close to zero, the whole thing falls apart.

Tools are what turn a model from something that can talk about your problem into something that can actually do something about it. A model that can only generate text is limited to giving you advice. Once it can search, run code, query a database, read files, or call an API, it can close the loop. It takes an action, sees what happened, and adjusts. That feedback loop is really where agentic behavior comes from.

What we've learned building these systems is that more tools isn't automatically better. If you hand a model fifty loosely defined tools, it gets confused about which one to use and when. The teams that get the most out of agents are pretty thoughtful about tool design. Clear names, clear descriptions, outputs that are actually legible to the model, and error messages that help it recover instead of just failing. In a lot of ways, designing tools for an agent is like designing an API for a new engineer on your team. If a smart person who just walked in the door couldn't figure out how to use it, the model probably can't either.

The other piece is that tools and context are really intertwined. A lot of the most valuable tools are the ones that let the agent go get its own context, so retrieval, search, looking at the codebase, rather than you trying to stuff everything into the prompt up front. That's been a big shift in how we think about it. Instead of engineering the perfect prompt, you give the agent the ability to explore, and you let it figure out what it needs.

And then there's trust. Every tool you give an agent is also a way for it to make a mistake in the real world. So part of the formula is thinking about permissions, which actions should be reversible, where a human needs to sign off. The agents that people actually rely on day to day tend to be the ones where that's been thought through carefully, not just the ones with the most capabilities.

r001.rationale: It describes a useful agent as combining a capable model with the right tools for the task.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss task-specific training or how much training is needed.

r003.rationale: It discusses agents using tools to act and gather context, but does not identify tool access during training as critical.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is, if you look at what makes an agent actually useful versus just a demo, it comes down to a few ingredients, and tool access is probably the one that gets underrated the most.

A language model on its own is basically a very smart brain in a jar. It can reason, it can write, it can plan, but it can't actually do anything in the world. Everything it knows is frozen at training time, and everything it produces is just text. Tools are what turn that into an agent. They're the hands and the eyes. Search gives it access to information it wasn't trained on. Code execution lets it actually compute things instead of guessing. A browser lets it interact with the systems people actually use. APIs let it take real actions, send the email, file the ticket, whatever it is.

What I think people miss is that the formula isn't just model plus tools. It's model plus tools plus the model actually being good at using those tools. And that second part turns out to be really hard. The early agent frameworks kind of assumed you could take a general-purpose model, hand it a list of function signatures, and it would figure it out. In practice you'd see it call the wrong tool, pass malformed arguments, not know when to stop, or get stuck in loops. So a huge amount of the progress over the last couple of years has been training models specifically to be good at tool use. Knowing when to call a tool versus answer from memory, how to recover when a call fails, how to chain many calls together over a long task without losing the thread.

The other piece is that the quality of the tools matters as much as the quality of the model. If you give an agent a flaky API with vague error messages, it's going to struggle the same way a new hire would. So a lot of the engineering work on our side has been making the environment legible to the model. Good descriptions, clear errors, sensible defaults, and limiting the surface area so the model isn't drowning in two hundred options.

And then, honestly, the last thing I'd say is that tool access is where the risk lives too. An agent that can only talk is low stakes. An agent that can run code and move money is a different thing. So you can't separate the capability question from the question of permissions, sandboxing, and when a human needs to be in the loop. Getting that right is as much a part of the formula as the model itself.

r001.rationale: It says useful agents combine a model that can reason and plan with tools that let it access information and take actions.

r002.rationale: It describes training models for tool use but does not say that a relatively small amount of task-specific training can teach the desired task.

r003.rationale: It discusses tool access and training models to use tools, but does not identify access to tools during training as critical.

astra-6.text:
I think tool access is a big part of what turns a language model into a useful agent. The model can reason about a task, but to actually accomplish it, it often needs to retrieve information, execute code, or take an action in another system. Tools provide that connection.

But access alone isn’t enough. The agent has to choose the right tool, supply the right inputs, interpret the result, and recover when something goes wrong. So the question isn’t just, “Can this model call an API?” It’s, “Can it reliably complete a task using the tools available to it?” That’s the level where you need to evaluate the whole system.

r002.rationale: It does not mention task-specific training or suggest that a small amount of training can teach the desired task.

r003.rationale: It describes tool access as useful for agents but does not identify access to tools during training as critical.

sol-6.1.text:
I think tool access is a really important part of what makes an agent useful. A language model on its own can give you an answer, but if you want it to actually accomplish something, it needs a way to interact with the world—retrieve information, run code, or take an action in another system.

But giving a model tools doesn’t automatically make it a useful agent. It has to choose the right tool, provide the right inputs, understand the result, and decide what to do next. And it needs to recognize when it doesn’t have enough information or should ask a person for help.

So I’d think about tool access as an enabling capability. The real question is whether the model can use those tools reliably enough to complete the task you care about.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent needs a language model plus tools to interact with the world and accomplish tasks, which conveys the model-and-tools combination.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss task-specific training or how much training is needed.

r003.rationale: It discusses an agent using tools to complete tasks, but does not say tools must be available during training.
